items.readable_text:
Content:
In some division problems, we do not obtain an exact result because there is a remainder. For example,

Content:
[MATH: 7 \div 4 = {\color{blue}{1}} \, \text{R} \, {\color{red}{3}}.]

Content:
This means that [MATH: 7 \div 4] is more than [MATH: 1,] but less than [MATH: 2.] It is somewhere in between.

Content:
So what is [MATH: 7\div 4] exactly?

Content:
We can write the exact result of this division problem as a mixed number, where the quotient ([MATH: {\color{blue}{1}}]) is the whole number part, and the remainder ([MATH: {\color{red}{3}}]) is expressed as a fraction.

Content:
To write the remainder as a fraction, we just need to divide it by the original divisor ([MATH: 4]). Therefore, expressed as a mixed number, our result is

Content:
[MATH: 7 \div 4 = {\color{blue}{1}} \, \dfrac{\color{red}3}{4}.]

sections.normalized_html: What is [MATH: 62 \div 9?]
sections.readable_text: What is [MATH: 62 \div 9?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The whole number part of [MATH: 62\div 9] must be [MATH: {\color{blue}6},] because

  • [MATH: 9] can go into [MATH: 62] a total of [MATH: {\color{blue}6}] times ([MATH: 9 \times {\color{blue}6} = 54]), but

  • [MATH: 9] cannot go into [MATH: 62] a total of [MATH: 7] times ([MATH: 9 \times 7 = 63]).

The remainder is [MATH: 62 - 54 = {\color{red}8},] so

[MATH: 62\div 9 = {\color{blue}{6}} \,\textrm{R}\, {\color{red}{8}}.]

To write the remainder as a fraction, we divide it by the original divisor ([MATH: 9]). Therefore,

[MATH: 62\div 9 = {\color{blue}6}\,\dfrac{\color{red}8}{9}\,.]

Content:
